Henry IV. Originally king of Navarre, he founded the Bourbon dynasty and ended the French Wars of Religion through compromise and pragmatism. His reign transformed France from decades of civil strife into a stable, prosperous kingdom.

He famously converted from Protestantism to Catholicism to win the French throne, saying that Paris was worth a mass. He chose unity and kingship over religious purity, and in 1598 he issued the Edict of Nantes, the most progressive religious settlement in early modern Europe. This edict guaranteed religious toleration for French Huguenots and finally ended the Wars of Religion.

From 1589 to 1610, Henry reigned over a remarkable transformation. Through careful fiscal management and the rebuilding of infrastructure, he took a war-torn kingdom and made it stable and prosperous. He was the first of the Bourbon dynasty, which ruled France and Spain for centuries and established his descendants permanently on the throne. He also sponsored exploration and colonization, including the founding of New France under Champlain, which extended French power overseas to what is now Quebec and Canada.

His reign ended abruptly in 1610 when the Catholic fanatic Ravaillac assassinated him. He died just as France was entering a new period of stability, leaving behind a son Louis XIII who inherited not just a crown, but a strong and unified kingdom.
